chief_complaint: tight band in palm pulling ring finger inward
hpi_details: 55-year-old male of Northern European descent complains of a slowly progressive, painless nodule in the palm of his right hand that has evolved into a tight cord. Over the last year, it has progressively pulled his ring and pinky fingers inward toward his palm, preventing him from fully extending them.
ideas: He thinks he may have torn or scarred an underlying tendon in his palm from decades of heavy yard work.
concerns: He is worried that his fingers will permanently curl into a fist and prevent him from gripping tools and shaking hands at work.
expectations: He hopes to receive a splint or an injection in the clinic today to help straighten his fingers back out.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Dupuytren Contracture is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Dupuytren Contracture: Tabletop test, collagenase injection or surgical aponeurectomy, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: tight band in palm pulling ring finger inward
Key HPI features: A 55-year-old man has a painless, slowly progressive palmar nodule and cord causing ring- and small-finger flexion contractures over a year.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Dupuytren Contracture.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Dupuytren Contracture.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Trigger finger (stenosing tenosynovitis) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Inability to place hand flat on table (Tabletop test positive).
management_principles: Plan for Dupuytren Contracture: Tabletop test, collagenase injection or surgical aponeurectomy
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 55M presenting with painless, progressive flexion contractures of the 4th and 5th digits of the right hand.
reference_soap.objective: Right hand exam reveals thickened, nodular cords in the palmar fascia extending to the ring and small fingers, causing a fixed 30-degree flexion contracture at the MCP and PIP joints. No pain on palpation.
reference_soap.plan: Refer to hand surgery or plastic surgery. Options include needle aponeurotomy, collagenase Clostridium histolyticum (Xiaflex) injection, or surgical fasciectomy, given the functional impairment and >30-degree contracture.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Dupuytren Contracture
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Dupuytren Contracture
Implement evidence-based management plan: Tabletop test, collagenase injection or surgical aponeurectomy

teaching.one_liner: Fibroproliferative disease of the palmar fascia causing fixed flexion contracture of the MCP and PIP joints.
red_flags: Rapid progression or function-limiting contracture requiring prompt hand-surgery assessment
New pain, erythema, warmth, or neurologic deficit suggesting a diagnosis other than Dupuytren disease

history.answer: I noticed a tight band in the palm of my right hand, and it has been pulling my ring and pinky fingers inward so I cannot straighten them out.
It started about a year ago as a firm little bump in my palm, and over time it thickened into a cord that began pulling my fingers down.
It is only in my right hand, specifically pulling down my ring finger and my little finger.
It feels like a thick, hard cord under the skin that physically tethers the fingers, holding both of them bent at about thirty degrees.
It has been gradually worsening over the past year. It does not come and go; it stays permanently bent.
No, there is no pain at all, even when I press on the cord or try to straighten my fingers.
No, they do not pop, snap, or lock up like a trigger finger. They are simply stuck bent and cannot extend all the way.
No, I have not had any numbness, tingling, or pins and needles in my hand.
No, I cannot lay my palm flat on a table anymore because the bent fingers hold my hand up.
No, I do not have any bumps on the soles of my feet or anywhere else, and my left hand is completely normal.
Nothing relieves it or makes it worse. Trying to forcefully stretch the fingers just feels tight and does not budge.
No, I have never had an injury, fracture, or laceration to this hand, and I do not work with vibrating power tools.
history.topic: History of hand trauma or vibration

history.answer: No, there is no redness, heat, or swelling anywhere on my hand.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or night sweats.
No, my weight has been completely steady.
I tried massaging the palm and doing gentle finger stretches at home, but it did not loosen the cord at all.
It makes it awkward to put my hand flat into my trouser pockets, and I keep poking myself when I try to wash my face.
I figured I must have strained or scarred a tendon in my palm from doing so much heavy yard work over the years.
I'm terrified that my fingers will freeze into a permanent claw and keep me from holding my tools or shaking clients' hands.
I was hoping you could give me a shot or fit me with a brace today to loosen this cord up.
I have always been healthy and do not have any chronic medical conditions.
No, I have never had diabetes, high blood sugar, or liver disease.
No, I have never had seizures, epilepsy, or taken anti-seizure medications.
None. I have never had any surgeries or hospital admissions.
I do not take any medications, over-the-counter pain relievers, or supplements.
I have no known allergies to medications or anything else.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only drink socially, maybe one or two beers or glasses of wine on the weekend.
I work as an office manager and live with my wife in an apartment.
My grandfather had bent fingers on his hands when he got older, but no one in my immediate family has been formally diagnosed.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, pulse 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, temperature 36.7°C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Well-nourished, well-groomed male in no acute physical distress.
Skin over the right palm shows thickened, puckered cords and firm subcutaneous nodules over the fourth and fifth rays, with no erythema, warmth, or ulceration.

Palpable non-tender nodular cord in the right palmar fascia extending to the fourth and fifth digits with fixed 30-degree flexion contractures at the MCP and PIP joints; unable to place the palm flat on the examination table (positive tabletop test).

Full active finger flexion bilaterally; active extension of the right fourth and fifth digits is mechanically restricted by the palmar cord, while intrinsic hand muscle strength remains 5/5 bilaterally.
Two-point discrimination and light touch sensation intact and symmetric across all digital nerve distributions of both hands.
Radial and ulnar pulses are 2+ bilaterally; capillary refill is under 2 seconds in all fingertips.
